intro: The “Black Keys” étude gives the right hand a nearly continuous stream of notes on the piano’s black keys while the left hand supplies harmonic direction and accents. In Edward Neeman’s recording, listen past the speed to the phrasing and to the different kinds of work done by the two hands.
question: Can you follow the left hand without losing the right hand’s continuous line?

sections.label: A′ · Opening figure returns
sections.mNote: the opening material returns after the central expansion

cues.title: The left hand directs
cues.text: The right hand’s rapid figuration uses the black keys almost throughout. Listen underneath it: the left hand supplies chords and accents that direct the harmony, rather than merely doubling the right-hand pattern.
cues.evidence: Technical premise of Op.10 No.5 in NIFC étude overview https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/gatunki/9_etiudy and work page https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/164. No claim that every note of both hands is a black key.

cues.title: Dedicated to Liszt
cues.text: Chopin dedicated the Op. 10 études to Franz Liszt. The dedication links the collection with another pianist-composer who treated virtuosity as a means of shaping concert music, not only as a display of speed.

cues.title: Hear phrases through the stream
cues.text: The rapid notes can make the surface seem uniform. Try following the larger rises, falls and cadences instead: a phrase can change direction even while the right hand continues its basic pattern.
cues.evidence: Listening invitation within the middle region; the report shows a broad level rise around 0:30–0:40, but does not establish individual score bars.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The collection of 1833
cues.text: Op. 10 was published in 1833, bringing twelve contrasting studies into one collection. The fifth étude’s particular keyboard pattern is one task among many, not a model for the whole book.

cues.title: Chopin’s modest description
cues.text: When Clara Wieck played this étude in Paris, Chopin wondered why she had chosen what he called a trifling piece. His reaction need not determine the listener’s judgement of the music’s invention or difficulty.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski reports Chopin’s reaction to Clara Wieck’s choice: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/164. Paraphrase, not an invented quotation.

cues.title: A compact final flourish
cues.text: The concluding stretch gathers the continuous motion into a short close. Listen for the larger accents and final chords rather than attempting to count every note of the right-hand figuration.
cues.evidence: Approximate coda region after the 1:26 report boundary; renewed louder windows at 1:30–1:40 precede the final decay.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The same figure changes its harmonic setting
transitions.how: The opening pattern continues into an expanding middle span rather than stopping for a slower contrasting melody. The left hand redirects the harmony and the weight of the accents while the right hand preserves the recognisable rapid figure. Continuity of texture makes the harmonic changes worth following.
transitions.evidence: Central region estimated around the 0:30 report boundary and the broad rise at 0:30–0:40. This label marks an approximate listening span, not a bar-aligned formal division.

transitions.title: The opening pattern recovers its home
transitions.how: The middle’s harmonic expansion gives way to the opening material in G♭ major. The right hand’s familiar kind of movement continues, so the return is easiest to recognise through the melodic contour, bass and harmonic destination rather than a sudden change of texture.
transitions.evidence: Approximate report boundary 1:00, after lower-level 0:50–0:55 windows; G-flat-coloured windows resume around 1:00. Formal return is estimated, not inferred solely from chroma.

transitions.title: The returning pattern becomes a closing gesture
transitions.how: The return is extended into a final flourish. Shorter gestures and enlarged accents bring the rapid surface to a close rather than preparing another episode. Listening to the left-hand foundations helps distinguish this concluding function from the similar figuration heard earlier.
transitions.evidence: Approximate late join at the 1:26 novelty peak, followed by renewed activity at 1:30–1:40 and final decay.

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
